questions.prompt: Why is complement called a 'bridge' between nonspecific and specific immunity?

options.text: It is made by both B cells and T cells working together
It can be triggered by common molecules (mannose, LPS) or by antibodies
It is part of the first line of defense along with the skin
It only works after vaccination has primed the immune system

questions.explanation: The trigger decides whether activation is specific or nonspecific.

questions.prompt: A Gram-negative bacterium enters the blood. Which of its molecules is most likely to trigger complement nonspecifically?

options.text: The plasmids carrying its accessory genes
Teichoic acid studding its thick cell wall
The 70S ribosomes inside its cytoplasm
Lipopolysaccharide in its outer membrane

questions.prompt: If a person lacked C3, which outcomes would be impaired most?

options.text: Histamine storage inside the vesicles of mast cells
Opsonization and the later steps that depend on C3b and C3a
Fever only, because C3 is the main pyrogen in the body
Interferon production by virus-infected neighboring cells

questions.explanation: C3b opsonizes and activates C5; C3a helps trigger mast cells.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes the membrane attack complex?

options.text: Interferon is released → AVPs are made → a pore forms → lysis
C9 coats the bacterium → a macrophage binds C9 → it engulfs the cell
C5b activates C6 → C7, C8, C9 join → C9 ring forms a pore → lysis
C3a binds mast cells → histamine is released → a pore forms → lysis

questions.explanation: Pores in the membrane burst the cell.

questions.prompt: Which statement about fever is FALSE?

options.text: Every fever should be lowered right away.
A fever near 44–46 °C could be fatal.
Some interleukins act as pyrogens.
Bacterial enzymes fail faster above 37 °C.
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamus thermostat.

questions.explanation: A low-grade fever can help fight infection.

questions.prompt: How do Toll-like receptors (Module 20) and nonspecific complement activation resemble each other?

options.text: Both recognize common microbial molecules such as mannose and LPS
Both require antibodies before they can recognize a microbe
Both are found only on red blood cells circulating in the blood
Both destroy viral RNA inside infected neighboring cells

questions.prompt: Mast cells can release histamine for several reasons. Which pair are both triggers covered in Modules 20–21?

options.text: Tissue damage and C3a/C5a binding
Fever and pyrogenic interleukins
Interferon binding and AVP production
Mannose binding and C9 ring formation

questions.explanation: Histamine can also be released in response to antibodies.

questions.prompt: Which second-line defense is described as working mainly against viruses rather than bacteria?

options.text: Lysozyme
Interferon
The membrane attack complex
Opsonization by C3b

questions.explanation: Most nonspecific defenses target bacteria; interferon targets viruses.

questions.prompt: A cell infected by a cold virus releases interferon. A flu virus later reaches a neighboring cell. What happens?

options.text: The neighbor is lysed by the MAC before the flu virus can enter it
The neighbor makes antibodies against flu, which neutralize it
Nothing happens, because interferon only protects against cold viruses
Its AVPs destroy the flu RNA too, because interferon is nonspecific

questions.explanation: Interferon doesn't care which virus it is.

questions.prompt: Why can't a cell keep making antiviral proteins all the time?

options.text: AVPs are toxic to neighboring cells and would kill the whole tissue
AVPs block histamine release, so inflammation could never start
AVPs destroy RNA in general, shutting down the cell's own proteins
AVPs raise body temperature to dangerous levels if they stay active

questions.explanation: That's also why interferon drugs have side effects.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of cytokine and role is correct?

options.text: Interferon — pyrogen; some interleukins — antiviral
Interleukin — opsonin; interferon — membrane attack
Both are complement proteins found in blood serum
Some interleukins — pyrogens; interferon — antiviral

questions.explanation: Two cytokines highlighted in the lecture.

questions.prompt: What does 'opsonize' literally mean, and why does it fit?

options.text: To warn — coating the microbe signals neighboring cells to make AVPs
To heat — coating the microbe triggers a pyrogenic fever
To cater (prepare for eating) — coated microbes are easier to eat
To burst — the membrane attack complex lyses the coated microbe

questions.prompt: A patient has a genetic defect in C9. Which outcome would fail?

options.text: Formation of the MAC pore
Interferon production
Histamine release from tissue damage
C3b opsonization

questions.prompt: Explain why a low-grade fever can help but a very high fever is dangerous, using enzyme activity curves.
questions.explanation: Human and bacterial enzymes both peak near 37 °C, but bacterial activity drops more steeply as temperature rises, so a low-grade fever impairs bacteria while our enzymes still work. Around 44–46 °C our own enzymes denature too, which can be fatal.

questions.prompt: Describe how complement activation leads to inflammation.
questions.explanation: C3 splits into C3a and C3b; C3b activates C5 (C5a + C5b); C3a and C5a bind receptors on mast cells, which release histamine → vasodilation, leaky vessels, redness, heat, swelling, pain, and WBC recruitment.
